Advanced Graphs

Graphs with negative edges, every pair of distances, one way groups, weak spots, pipes full of water, a search with a sense of direction and a walk over every edge. Each idea comes with a playful animation you can step through.

Part 1

➖Negative edges and Bellman-Ford

Dijkstra settles a node for good the moment it is popped. That is only safe when every edge is positive. With a negative edge, a longer detour can turn out cheaper, and Dijkstra never looks back. Bellman-Ford is slower but patient: it relaxes every edge, again and again, for n − 1 rounds.

relax(u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v] then dist[v] = dist[u] + w
A shortest path uses at most n − 1 edges, so n − 1 rounds are enough. If a distance still drops in one extra round, the graph has a negative cycle and no shortest path exists.
Bellman-Ford costs O(V E). Network routers that use the distance vector idea, such as the old RIP protocol, share distances with their neighbours in the same way.
Part 2

🗺️All pairs with Floyd-Warshall

Sometimes you need the distance between every pair of places, like a road atlas table. Floyd-Warshall fills an n × n matrix with three nested loops. In round k, every pair i, j asks one question: is going through node k shorter than what I have?

d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j])   for k, then i, then j
It handles negative edges too. A negative number on the diagonal at the end means a negative cycle. Swapping + and min for "and" and "or" gives reachability, which LeetCode 1462 uses.
Part 3

🫧Strongly connected components

In a directed graph, a strongly connected component is a largest group of nodes where every node can reach every other node. Kosaraju's algorithm finds them with two depth first searches. Pass 1 records the order in which nodes finish. Pass 2 reverses every edge and starts from the latest finisher. Each search in pass 2 stays trapped inside exactly one component.

Squashing each component into one node always leaves a graph with no cycles. Compilers use this to find groups of modules that depend on each other, and 2-SAT solvers use it to decide whether a set of rules can all hold.
Part 4

🌉Bridges and articulation points

A bridge is an edge whose removal splits the graph in two. An articulation point, or cut point, is a node whose removal does. One depth first search finds both. Each node gets a discovery time d, and a low value l: the smallest discovery time its subtree can reach with one back edge.

Test after visiting child v of uMeaning
l[v] > d[u]the edge u-v is a bridge
l[v] ≥ d[u], u is not the rootu is a cut point
the root has 2 or more childrenthe root is a cut point
The Graphs chapter practice problem Critical Connections asks for exactly these bridges.
Part 5

🚰Maximum flow and minimum cut

Each pipe has a capacity. How much water per second can flow from the source s to the sink t? Edmonds-Karp repeats one step: find the shortest path from s to t where every pipe still has room, and push as much as the tightest pipe allows. Pushing also opens a reverse pipe, so a later path can take back flow that was badly placed.

Max flow equals min cut. When no path is left, the nodes still reachable from s form one side of a cut, and the full pipes crossing it add up to exactly the maximum flow.
Edmonds-Karp costs O(V E²). Matching students to projects or workers to jobs is a flow problem: one unit of capacity per person and per job.
Part 6

⭐A* search: Dijkstra with a sense of direction

Dijkstra spreads out evenly in every direction. A* adds a guess h of the distance still to go, and always expands the open node with the smallest f = g + h, where g is the distance travelled so far. On a grid with four moves, the Manhattan distance is a good guess.

f(n) = g(n) + h(n)    Manhattan h = |row − goal row| + |col − goal col|
The guess must never overestimate the real distance. If it does, A* can return a path that is not the shortest. With h = 0, A* is exactly Dijkstra.
Part 7

✏️Euler paths with Hierholzer

An Euler circuit uses every edge exactly once and returns to the start. Leonhard Euler asked this about the seven bridges of Königsberg in 1736. In a directed graph it exists when every node has in degree equal to out degree and all edges belong to one connected piece. Hierholzer's algorithm walks unused edges until it gets stuck, writes the stuck node down, steps back, and continues. The answer comes out reversed.

An Euler path, which may end somewhere else, needs one node with out − in = 1 as the start and one with in − out = 1 as the end. LeetCode 332 Reconstruct Itinerary is this problem with airport names.
